meta.title: Who really said "If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Abraham Maslow never wrote it. His 1966 book says something longer, and the law behind it was Abraham Kaplan’s. The paraphrase traced and dated.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail'?
meta.ogDescription: Maslow wrote a hammer-and-nail line in 1966 — but not this one. The compressed version has no author, and the idea was Kaplan's first.

answer.label: Not Maslow’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: Maslow did write a hammer-and-nail sentence — but not this one. In The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (Harper & Row, 1966) he wrote, “I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail.” The snappier “if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail” is a later compression with no documented author, and the underlying law of the instrument was Abraham Kaplan’s, in print before Maslow’s book.

source.trailTitle: How a hedged sentence became a proverb
trail: February 1962 — the law, without the nail. Abraham Kaplan, a philosophy professor at UCLA, gave a banquet speech at the American Educational Research Association meeting. A report published that June in the Journal of Medical Education carries what Quote Investigator calls the earliest strong match ↗ it has found: “Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded.”

1963 — the nail appears. In Computer Simulation of Personality, the psychologist Silvan Tomkins wrote, “If one has a hammer one tends to look for nails” — the first citation in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ to pair the two objects, though the phrasing is still not the modern one.

1966 — Maslow’s version. The Psychology of Science gives the sentence that is closest to what circulates today, and the one Wikiquote lists as sourced ↗: “I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail.”

1981–1984 — the compression, and the wrong author. Quote Investigator records “everything looks like a nail” as a 1981 book chapter title and in Warren Buffett’s 1984 Columbia essay, and then an August 1984 letter to InfoWorld ↗ printing the short form under the heading “Twain Said It.”
source.excerptNote: Note the hedge — “I suppose it is tempting” — and the verb “treat,” not “looks like.” The popular version drops both.

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.heading: About Abraham Maslow
author.metaLine: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, founder of humanistic psychology
author.bio: Abraham Harold Maslow (1 April 1908 – 8 June 1970) was an American psychologist who taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University and founded the humanistic psychology movement. He is best known for Maslow’s hierarchy of needs and the idea of self-actualization. His 1966 book The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance argued against a science that puts method before question — and it is where he reached for the hammer that now carries his name.

cite.sourceCitation: Abraham H. Maslow, The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (New York: Harper & Row, 1966), 15–16. The popular short wording is a later paraphrase; the earliest strong match for the adage known to Quote Investigator is a report of Abraham Kaplan’s February 1962 speech in the Journal of Medical Education 37 (June 1962): 637.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: This adage has been handed to almost everyone. The reference expert Ralph Keyes summed it up in The Quote Verifier: credit “has been given to everyone from Buddha to Bernard Baruch.” Here is what each claim is actually worth.

items.why: “If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail” appears in none of Maslow’s works. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ records the compressed shape only from the 1980s — a 1981 Howard J. Ruff chapter title and Warren Buffett’s 1984 “to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail” — with no named originator.

The UCLA philosopher named it the law of the instrument. A report of his February 1962 banquet speech, published that June in the Journal of Medical Education, gives the earliest strong match Quote Investigator has found: “Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded.” He restated it in The Conduct of Inquiry (1964), p. 28 ↗. Kaplan’s versions have no nail in them.

Twain is the most common recipient and, as Keyes puts it, the credit rests on “no evidence whatsoever” ↗. The earliest Twain credit in Quote Investigator’s record is a reader’s letter to InfoWorld in August 1984 — long after Maslow’s book.
Wiktionary ↗ notes the phrase was labelled “Baruch’s Observation” in The Complete Murphy’s Law (1991). Neither the Baruch nor the Buddha claim is supported by any documented source.

misattribution.truthLine: The law is Kaplan’s, the hammer-and-nail pairing was already in print with Silvan Tomkins in 1963, and the wording closest to the modern saying is Maslow’s — but the sentence everyone repeats belongs to none of them. See Quote Investigator’s full trace ↗.

context.heading: Why Maslow reached for a hammer
lead: Maslow’s hammer is not a line about carpentry. It sits inside a book-length argument that orthodox science had begun to organise itself around its techniques rather than its questions — that researchers were choosing problems to suit the methods they already knew how to run. The sentence arrives as the second half of an image: Maslow describes an elaborate automatic car wash that did a beautiful job of washing automobiles, and treated everything else that fell into its clutches as an automobile to be washed.

That is the joke and the warning together. The tool is not stupid; it is excellent, and its excellence is the problem. Abraham Kaplan had already named the effect the law of the instrument ↗ — “Give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding” — but Kaplan’s boy pounds; he never meets a nail. Maslow’s sentence does — Silvan Tomkins had paired the two objects three years earlier — and it is Maslow’s wording that the world remembered.
detailsBody: Maslow’s sentence is hedged and conversational — “I suppose it is tempting” — and hedges are the first thing an adage sheds. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the compressed shape hardening in print through the early 1980s: Howard J. Ruff used “When You Have a Hammer in Your Hand, Everything Looks Like a Nail” as a 1981 chapter title, and Warren Buffett used “to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail” in his 1984 Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville essay, crediting it only to “a friend.”

Once a saying loses its author it acquires a better one. By August 1984 a letter to InfoWorld was printing “If the only tool you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail” and confidently handing it to Mark Twain.
context.pull: The tool is not stupid. Its excellence is the problem.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator documents the full chronology: Kaplan's February 1962 banquet speech reported June 1962 in the Journal of Medical Education ('Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded', no 'nail'); Tomkins 1963 ('If one has a hammer one tends to look for nails'); Kaplan's Conduct of Inquiry 1964 p.28; Maslow's The Psychology of Science 1966 pp.15-16 ('I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail'); Ruff's 1981 chapter title 'When You Have a Hammer in Your Hand, Everything Looks Like a Nail'; Buffett 1984 'to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail'; August 1984 InfoWorld letter 'Twain Said It'; and Ralph Keyes' verdict that the Twain credit rests on 'no evidence whatsoever' and that credit has been given 'to everyone from Buddha to Bernard Baruch'. QI concludes Maslow's 1966 version is the one similar to popular modern expressions.

Wikiquote lists the hammer sentence in its sourced 1960s section with the exact wording 'I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail', cited to The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (1966), ch. 2, p. 15; and gives Maslow's dates as April 1, 1908 - June 8, 1970.

Wikipedia's 'Law of the instrument' article gives Kaplan's 1964 The Conduct of Inquiry p. 28 wording ('Give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding') alongside Maslow's 1966 The Psychology of Science pp. 15-16 wording, and notes earlier antecedents including the 1868 Once a Week passage.

Wikipedia gives Maslow's birth date as April 1, 1908 and death as June 8, 1970, describes him as an American psychologist known for the hierarchy of needs and for founding humanistic psychology, notes he taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University, and states he is known for 'Maslow's hammer' from The Psychology of Science (1966), popularized as 'if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail'.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of 'The psychology of science; a reconnaissance' by Abraham H. Maslow, Harper & Row, New York, 1966, as an access-restricted lending-library item.
Open Library's catalogue record confirms 'The psychology of science: a reconnaissance' by Abraham H. Maslow was published by Harper & Row in New York in 1966.

Wiktionary's etymology attributes the modern formulation to Maslow's 1966 The Psychology of Science (p. 15), notes Kaplan's similar 1964 'law of the instrument' from The Conduct of Inquiry p. 28, records that the phrase was labelled 'Baruch's Observation' after Bernard Baruch in The Complete Murphy's Law (1991), and states it is often attributed without citation to Mark Twain.
